# Conclusion {#sec-chapter6}

The three research questions posed at the outset each have a direct answer. This chapter states those answers, reflects on what they establish and where they fall short, and identifies what a researcher or practitioner building on this work would need to address next.

## Research Summary

This study set out to close a specific gap: the absence of a quantitative, service-level instrument for prioritising technical debt in vendor-dominated trading IT, where source code is largely inaccessible and code-centric tools therefore cannot operate. Following a Design Science approach [@hevnerDesignScienceInformation2004; @peffersDesignScienceResearch2007], five operational indicators were derived from the literature, mapped to technical debt dimensions (@tbl-indicators-lit), and operationalised from two years of live ITSM and CMDB records at a regulated Swiss trading institution. A TOPSIS model ranked six production services under two weight configurations and two observation years. The evaluation in @sec-chapter5 then tested the ranking from five directions: weight sensitivity and its Monte Carlo extension across the full weight space, temporal comparison, convergent validity against SAW and VIKOR, discriminant value against an incident-only baseline, and structural rigour under service removal, including a rank-reversal-free absolute-mode variant. The artefact works in the sense the pragmatist stance of @sec-chapter3 demands: it produces a defensible, reproducible ordering from data the organisation already holds.

## Findings Against Research Questions

**RQ1** asked how technical debt in mission-critical trading systems can be prioritised quantitatively at the service level using operational data. The framework itself is the answer. Five indicators, three from ITSM records and two from the CMDB, feed a TOPSIS model whose closeness coefficient orders services by debt priority without any recourse to source code. The method choice is not incidental: the discriminant test showed that the multi-criteria ordering diverges substantially from an incident-only view ($\tau = 0.600$ in 2025, $0.200$ in 2024), and the divergence falls exactly where it should. SVC-02, whose 1,221 unsupported component months are invisible to an incident count, rises; SVC-05, whose incident volume is offset by a clean infrastructure profile, falls.

**RQ2** asked to what extent operational service management metrics serve as valid proxies for technical debt severity. The honest answer is: to a demonstrable but bounded extent. The rankings match the debt profiles the literature predicts for each position. SVC-04's combination of the highest incident load with a clean infrastructure record reads as architectural and process debt, SVC-02's profile as concentrated infrastructure lifecycle debt, and SVC-03 as a reference case for a well-maintained service. Convergent validity supports this reading, since SAW and VIKOR reproduce the same high-priority and low-priority halves and the same lowest-ranked service in every configuration. What the evaluation cannot establish is criterion validity, because no independent measure of non-code debt exists to validate against. The proxy relationship therefore retains the status it was given in @sec-chapter1: a hypothesis that survived every test available within this design, not a proven law.

**RQ3** asked how stable the rankings are under weight perturbation. Stable at the extremes, sensitive in the middle. The two discrete configurations agree strongly ($\tau = 0.867$ in 2025), and the Monte Carlo extension across 20,000 sampled weightings shows SVC-03 in last place in 99.1% of them, with the top cluster of SVC-04, SVC-06 and SVC-02 holding the leading positions in the large majority. Sensitivity concentrates in the middle ranks and in the identity of the single top service, where TOPSIS favours SVC-04 while SAW and VIKOR favour SVC-06. As @sec-absolutemode showed, that disagreement is not noise but a substantive difference in how methods treat a debt profile concentrated in few criteria, and it marks the boundary between what the framework settles and what remains a managerial judgement.

## Contribution to Knowledge

The contribution is threefold. First, to the best of current knowledge, this is the first application of TOPSIS to live ITSM and CMDB records for technical debt prioritisation in financial trading IT, addressing the absence of validated quantitative multi-criteria approaches that @lenarduzziSystematicLiteratureReview2021 identified across the field. Second, the study contributes an operationally defined indicator set with an explicit literature mapping to debt dimensions, together with evidence on how that set behaves under four evaluation strands. Third, and less anticipated at the outset, the evaluation yielded a methodological finding of independent interest: sample-relative methods and the absolutely anchored TOPSIS variant respond differently to concentrated debt profiles, and the 2024 data show that this difference is consequential for the top of a ranking. The resulting division of labour, with the standard formulation triangulated against SAW and VIKOR as the primary signal and absolute mode contributing rank-reversal immunity and cross-period comparability, is a transferable design lesson for MCDM applications beyond this case.

## Practical Contribution

For the case organisation and comparable institutions, the framework converts data that already sits in routine ITSM and CMDB records into an auditable priority ordering, which matters in an environment where FINMA Circular 2023/1 requires demonstrable ICT operational risk management [@finmaCircular202312024]. The instrument surfaces precisely the debt that current governance is most likely to miss: SVC-02 appears stable on incident metrics alone while carrying the portfolio's largest infrastructure lifecycle exposure. Two conditions on use follow from this study rather than qualifying it. The scores are ordinal decision-support signals, not measurements of debt, and they describe services, not teams; as agreed in the governance scope (@sec-ethics), high-debt profiles typically reflect historical design decisions rather than the competence of current custodians [@ahmadTechnicalDebtNot2026].

## Limitations and Future Work

The limitations documented in @sec-datalimitations and @sec-evaluationlimitations frame what remains to be done. The six-service demonstration set was selected for data completeness, limits the power of the rank-correlation tests, and shares its dataset with the framework's construction, so the evaluation establishes robustness and method-independence rather than criterion validity. The design is cross-sectional, the CFR indicator shares its incident numerator with incident frequency, and recording-practice variation across teams can compress the scores of services where informal incident handling is common.

Four directions follow directly. The first is external validation: applying the framework in other regulated organisations to test whether the proxy hypothesis holds beyond this case. The second is longitudinal evaluation, tracking whether services ranked as high priority go on to generate the operational and financial consequences the debt literature predicts [@bankerTechnicalDebtFirm2020], which would move the proxy claim from plausible to evidenced. The third is portfolio-wide deployment once indicator coverage across the remaining services is complete, which would also strengthen the statistical footing of the stability tests. The fourth concerns the absolute-mode variant, whose fixed criterion bounds currently rest on organisational thresholds; deriving those bounds from regulatory or cross-industry reference points would make its cross-period scores comparable between organisations as well as between years.

## Reflective Note

Two aspects of this study turned out differently from what I expected at the outset. I anticipated that the main difficulty would be computational; it was instead definitional, since deciding what an incident count or a derived change failure rate can legitimately be taken to mean consumed far more effort than implementing the model that consumes them. I also expected the alternative methods to serve as a simple confirmation exercise, whereas the disagreement between them over SVC-06 became one of the more instructive results of the thesis, forcing an explicit position on whether debt dimensions are compensatory. The discipline of Design Science helped in both cases: by demanding that every design decision be justified and every evaluation strand be specified in advance, it kept the study honest about the difference between what the artefact demonstrates and what it merely suggests. The framework does not measure technical debt. It orders services by the operational shadow debt casts, and within the limits stated above, it does so reproducibly, defensibly and in a form a regulated institution can act on.
